posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
I continue to second-guess myself on what my first real RPG Maker game should be. As a writer, choosing what story to write next is a problem I’m used to having, but since the process of game-making is much more complex, the decision is pretty paralyzing in that context.
It’s not helped by the fact that I have all kinds of different ideas for games of various formats. So I was thinking it might be helpful to group these ideas into categories and then ask for people’s opinions on those categories. Not expecting it to outright solve the problem for me, but it can’t hurt to gather data.
Really I’d appreciate any kind of comment, but here are a few potential questions to consider: What kind of game would you recommend for a first project*? Do any of the below categories sound particularly appealing or unappealing to you? Do you feel there are too many games of a certain type already out there, or maybe even too few?
*Technically I've had a number of previous projects, but except for a few false starts I haven't put serious work in on the editor since XP was the latest platform.
Anyway, here are the options I’m currently considering (I can go into more detail if necessary):
Standard epic(?) JRPG. The player has a party of characters that goes on a quest, fights enemies, etc.
A game somewhat inspired by open-world games, where the plot takes a back seat to exploration. Probably will have just a single playable character, though I’ll have to find ways to make combat interesting.
Game where the player constructs parties from a roster of playable characters that they can send into a number of different small worlds instead of just one big one.
Game with the same type of party construction as #3, but with a set up more like Adventure Mode in
Hyrule Warriors
, going around a grid-based world map and fighting a series of battles at each screen/square.
Contemporary fantasy game where the protagonists fight using a variety of summoned beings.
Spooky game that will probably involve puzzles and maybe some light combat.
Spooky game that’s more of a “walking simulator,” where the player character moves through a series of dream-like scenes.
Games in any of the above categories that primarily make use of RTP material. These have a certain appeal to me as someone with no artistic or musical talent, despite their obvious limitations. On the other hand, it would probably be difficult to convince people to give RTP-based games a shot, no matter how creatively the resources are used.
And I think that's about it, since other ideas are too vague at this point. Thanks for reading! Looking forward to hearing people's thoughts.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
This is all just my personal opinion, so take it with a grain of salt.
TMS said:
What kind of game would you recommend for a first project*?
Click to expand...
Broadly speaking, I would say a first project in a new engine should be something small enough to complete a
first draft prototype
(that's playable from beginning to end) in a couple of months. This prototype doesn't necessarily need to be the entire game – if you're planning a longer game, it could just be the first chapter.
One of the reasons for this is that, if it can be completed in such a short time, you can build the prototype entirely within the trial period for the engine
before buying it
, which means you could decide you don't really like the engine after all and decide to scrap the project and not buy it.
I would also say a first project should be as simple as possible. While it's hard to judge from so little details, numbers 6 and 7 on your list sound the closest to satisfying this – something that could probably be prototyped with no or few plugins, that could be playable from beginning to end within a couple of months. Number 3 might also work, if you limit the number of "small worlds" to, say, 3 or 4 for the prototype stage.
And, I would say a first project should
definitely
use the RTP, at least initially. I think the RTP receives a lot of undeserved hate, so I wouldn't avoid it solely on the basis that "it would probably be difficult to convince people to give RTP-based games a shot"; or rather, I don't think that's a true statement. I think it really comes down to how creatively the resources are used. Note that this includes potentially editing the RTP in minor ways to suit your game – for example, in the Inside C tilesheet, you could slightly rearrange the bottles and glasses, recolour the red "potion bottle", adjust the position of the book on the altar, etc, to better suit how you want to use them in your maps. (You could do such edits in-place, or you could paste them into a D or E tilesheet and do them there.)
(Full disclosure: the game I'm working on now is almost entirely RTP, edits of RTP, or graphics based on RTP, eg a custom-made sprite of a battler that didn't have an RTP sprite. I also have tentative plans for another game that would probably use all the RTP terrain and maybe a few enemy battlers, but replace everything else with custom art.)

posts.author: Phantasmagoric
posts.body:
Don't do it like me, trying to make an ambitious project from the get-go. I too have several story ideas, and many of them I even already started making, but you will lose the initial hype after a while, and after that, you need to rely on your own determination and belief in your project to get it to the end.
I have paralyzed my larger projects in favor of doing a smaller - though still kinda ambitious in some senses, I admit - more realistic project so that I can maybe get a little more of a name for myself (don't put too many expectations on yourself too much, neither me or you are likely to be the next indie sensation of the year. You may frustrate yourself) in the community before launching a bigger project. I have confidence in my ideas, I believe I can make something people will like, even if I don't gather a massive fanbase, it's okay.
At the end of the day, it's about making the game you'd want to play, tell the story you want to tell, share your vision and have fun with your peers.
That all being said... about your list of projects, here's a suggestion: why not mix some of them? Try to cut that list in half by fusing some ideas. That will even help you make each idea more unique and complex. Here are my suggestions
2+3+5: Single protagonist, every other "Party member" is a summon; contemporary, with an "Open world" that is actually a set of smaller worlds you can fully explore
1+3: Epic JRPG with grid combat
6+7: Spooky dream simulator with puzzles
8: While I myself like the idea of testing one's narrative talents by making a story with the RTP, it
might not be very well seen by a large portion of the player base. Check my
latest post
about exactly that.

posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
Seems like the common thread here is to stick to something manageable at first, which makes sense.
@Solar_Flare
I particularly like the idea of prototyping a game, which I hadn't really considered before. Before my recent hesitation started, the game I was considering to use as my first fell under categories 3 and 8, tentatively titled
Vanquishers.
I suppose I could go with that after all, in prototype form, with only the first couple worlds (eight or nine is the end goal) and the first few characters. I'm trying to let the RTP limitation inform the game's themes, but was wondering if I should start with something more original and ambitious lest no one care to play it. If I do go with
Vanquishers
while relying primarily on the RTP, I'll at least make whatever edits I can to suit my needs and tastes.
@Phantasmagoric
Mixing categories is something worth considering. In many cases it's not possible according to my current ideas. Most of the categories I mentioned in the first post are tied to a specific idea for a game or game series. The only real exception (besides 8) is 4, which was a conception I originally came up with for a fan game that I'm now unsure if I should bother making. For the rest, I could try mix-and-matching, but only if I'm willing to shake up my current plans. I guess there's also a game idea I have that I'm not sure what category or combination of categories it should go in, so that's something to think about.
@alice_gristle
I'm sure you're right. It's just a mental block of mine, since I want to work on every game at once, which means none of them will ever get done. Probably I'll just need to pick one to prioritize, and then work on the rest as I have time.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
TMS said:
Really I’d appreciate any kind of comment, but here are a few potential questions to consider: What kind of game would you recommend for a first project*?
Click to expand...
Something small, few features, the player can complete it in under 3 hours.  Finishing a game is more important than building a perfect one.  Scaled down games can be great.  Even ones the player can complete in fewer than 5 hours can be great experiences.
Completing smaller games is also great practice for doing longer ones.
Works the same with writing, does it not?  Do you go into each new idea with the thought of creating a 500 page epic, with 6 sequels?  Or, do you just start writing the story and it ends when it ends?
I started writing with smaller projects first.  Because a completed story is worth more than one that isn't.  So, a two page story about a Dragon and a Princess was my first work.  Written for a friend who was sick at the time.
I mostly write "short stories" these days (as I can complete them) of a length of 10-25 pages.  I occasionally work on 100 page projects (though few ever see completion).  I'm not ready yet to write my "magnum opus", but someday I will be.  It will probably be a sprawling 300+ page affair.  But, I'm not good enough yet for that, nor committed enough.
TMS said:
Do any of the below categories sound particularly appealing or unappealing to you? Do you feel there are too many games of a certain type already out there, or maybe even too few?
Click to expand...
If it's a good game, I'd give it a shot.  Short of specific genres that have nothing on offer to me, personally, I don't snub most games.  I don't do fighting games, or most racing games.  I don't do "twitch reflex arena shooters" either or most MOBA games (I find their design philosophies to be completely abhorrent and bass-ackwards in terms of execution and design, with few rare exceptions.  Yes, I think LoL is absolutely designed like garbage, even if people are having fun with it).

They're fine avenues for a "first game".
Here's what I'd recommend you do:
Which of these are you the most passionate about?  Which one are you most committed to?  Start there.
It's the same with writing stories, to be honest.  I want to tell a story about X, so I write about X.  All other options are off the table until I finish it.  Or, completely lose interest, since I explored everything I wanted/needed to.
I got some writing advice once that I've sort of treasured ever since.  I apply it to a lot of my own life.  Maybe it's appropriate to share it here:
"If you don't have anything to say, then don't say anything."  In reference to me trying to force a story where there wasn't one.  I didn't have anything to say, so why was I opening my mouth and expending so much effort on saying something?
I think it applies to game design, too.
If something doesn't have a purpose in a game, and you're not "saying something" with it, then why are you designing it?  Why force your mouth open and words to come out when you have nothing to say?

TMS said:
What kind of game would you recommend for a first project*?
Click to expand...
When I started using rpg maker, I was a bit overwhelmed with the amount of stories and games I wanted to make. I knew I shouldn't get too ambitious, so I came up with short, simple stories. I also joined game jams aimed at beginners so I could get used to using the engine. But make sure you like the story you go with! Game dev will become a slog if you aren't 100% passionate about the story you're telling.
For my
first game
, I made a simple puzzle game. Nothing too special, it was mostly just for me to get used to switches, variables and eventing.
Get to know the engine first before you go off onto more ambitious projects.
And if any other ideas come up, write them down and set them to the side so you can return to them in the future

It depends on what I'm writing, to be honest, but in general I do set out simply to tell a certain story, without setting expectations or requirements ahead of time as to how long it will wind up. Video games are a little different, though, I feel. Most games are more than just a story. The story is usually a skeleton while the gameplay acts as the meat on it, so that most games are bigger or take longer than they would need to be simply to tell the story. The player has to have plenty to actually do. And really I have so many ideas that it's hard to pick and choose just what and how much to include in a single game.
Tai_MT said:
Which of these are you the most passionate about?  Which one are you most committed to?  Start there.

Unfortunately, it varies from day to day, and sometimes hour to hour. What I do with my writing is just pick a specific story, lock in on it, and then work on it for at least a little while every day whether I feel like it or not. Probably I'll have to do the same with my game projects.

Starting in novel form certainly is an option for a more story-heavy game (though it would be a little easier to translate to game format if you started in stage play form instead, but still). posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
@Solar_Flare

The story I'm currently novelizing was actually pretty simple, which is why I initially chose it for a "first"
RPG Maker
project. But I got discouraged with the game early on, since I didn't really have the artistic skills to do it justice, and so I settled for telling the story in my usual medium, hoping that once it was done I could use it to interest other people in the project. That was well over a year ago now. (770,000 words in several months is highly impressive, by the way, no matter how rough the draft. I struggle to find the time and willpower to write, and when I do I only average about 10 words per minute.) Now I've kind of fallen away from that kind of thinking. I don't know if I'll ever make that novel into a game. If I do, it probably won't be a 1:1 adaptation.
As far as standard JRPGs go, I'm currently leaning toward having a kind of sandbox feel to them, allowing the player to explore the world as a party of one, with occasional temporary guest characters, and probably some summons the player can use at any time. The big difficulty conception-wise will be coming up with a reason for the player avatar to be adventuring largely at random. Of course, the biggest overall issue (besides my work ethic), will be getting the resources that I'll need made.

posts.author: Darkmoon9
posts.body:
Do whatever project you are the most motivated to be working on. Motivation is the primary factor in making sure a game actually gets completed.
I actually started out making a liniar story based rpg thats bases on an old novel of mine. Is about 30-40 hours long and took me about 2 years to make. It is possible to complete a bigger project as your first game if you are motivated and determined enough.
But thats the key factor here, motivation, work on whatever idea you are least likely to give up on in a few months time. A game is more than just game mechanics, try presenting a story you want to tell. One that is important to you.
The biggest enemy to the completion of your project is losing interest in making it.

posts.author: FrostGiant32
posts.body:
If this is your first serious project in a long time, I'd honestly recommend picking the idea with the smallest scope rather than the one that sounds the most exciting. Finishing a game teaches far more than endlessly planning one. From your list, the spooky puzzle-focused concept or the exploration-focused game with a single protagonist seem like the safest choices.
One thing I've noticed is that players often appreciate games with a clear core idea. For example, I recently tried the Chicken Road app, and despite being much simpler than an RPG, it works because the concept is immediately understandable and easy to expand upon. The Chicken Road iOS version is a good example of how a focused idea can be more effective than dozens of mechanics. Sometimes the best first project is the one that does a few things really well rather than trying to become the next epic JRPG. If you're curious, the
chicken road ios
release is worth a look from a game-design perspective.

posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
Thanks for the further replies!
@Solar_Flare
:
If I were to adapt the novel outright, it would probably resemble my original conception for the game. One big difference is that in the game the player would probably accumulate party members and stick with them from the moment they join, whereas in the novel I’ve allowed the main characters greater independence. And the game would presumably have side quests the novel didn’t cover, and of course more random encounters, etc. Naturally the dialogue, too, would be reworked as necessary.
@Darkmoon9
:
You make a great point about motivation. My problem is that my motivation as regards any one project is a very fickle thing. Typically, the thing I’m most excited about is whatever I happen
not
to be working on at the moment. It’s why I’ve eventually settled for just picking a project or two and sticking to them until they’re done. I remember my one foray into fan fiction some 16 years ago, where I started out writing several novel chapters a day, but soon settled into a pattern of taking a month or more just to complete one. But I kept at it, and finished the damn thing eventually. Seems like it’s the same story with all of my creative work. As I get older and start seeing my deficiencies more clearly, I become less capable of moving quickly. More on that later.
@FrostGiant32
:
Your advice is a little at variance with Darkmoon9’s, but is equally solid. Easier to finish something that’s less ambitious, and it would form a good experiential foundation for later, more elaborate efforts. Thanks for looking over the range of ideas and giving a definite opinion on the options!
Now that I’m caught up on replies, I have a bit of an update on where I’m at with this whole thing. I’ve been thinking lately about how life is short and my rate of production is slow. It’s made me think that maybe for the foreseeable future I should stick to what I’m best at (writing fiction), since there’s no way I’m going to get around to everything I want to do, and if I’m going to pour a bunch of time into a project it should be one I have the greatest chance of doing justice to. This, of course, kind of argues against my trying to make video games (or card games, which I’m also interested in). It’s doubtful that I could make anything worthwhile on my own in that line. The ideal situation would be to team up with a group of people from different creative backgrounds who could collaborate to bring one of my ideas to life, but finding people with both the necessary talents and the necessary interest and motivation seems about as unlikely as a million-dollar budget falling into my lap.
Maybe novelizations like the one I’m currently working on could be used eventually as a recruiting tool, though getting anyone to read one’s work (if it’s not fan fiction, anyway) is like pulling teeth; salesmanship is not a job I’m apparently cut out for. But at any rate, writing feels like it has a greater chance of ultimate success than tackling a game on my own just now. Besides, I’ve been dreaming about making a game using
RPG Maker
for two decades. Seems like if I had the requisite skill and passion to do it alone, I wouldn’t still be hovering around the starting line.
I might start another thread sometime on the topic of recruiting people for collaborative projects, but meanwhile I’d love to keep discussion going here, even if an ultimate decision on what game to attempt first seems further than ever.

posts.author: Milennin
posts.body: For a first project, the recommendation is to make something small in scale to learn the engine and to actually finish something instead of being stuck making something too ambitious for many years. The low stakes setting makes for a good place to experiment with story elements that you've never tried or considered before, just to broaden your writing horizon. At least, that's what I did for my first game and it was a fun experience.
